rows.grounds: the instruments and the qualities beginning with smallness
and the manifold of cognitive states
beginning with sattva, belonging to them

items.question: What arises from the unmanifest and belongs to these givers of yoga?
premises: The organs and powers such as smallness are effects.
The expansion of cognitions also arises from the unmanifest.
The strands beginning with sattva belong to these beings.
items.inference: The unmanifest gives rise to instruments, powers, cognitions, and the strands that characterize these yogic givers.
uncertainties: The exact referent of amīṣām is supplied from the preceding verse.
items.plain_english: From the unmanifest arise the organs, the powers such as smallness, the various effects, the whole range of cognitions, and the strands beginning with sattva that belong to them.

rows.grounds: the four qualities: merit, knowledge, dispassion, and lordship
these beings, arising from the strands

items.question: What do the givers of yoga bestow upon individual souls?
premises: The givers of yoga arise in relation to the strands.
They bestow merit, knowledge, dispassion, and lordship.
They also bestow the various fruits of those qualities.
items.inference: The givers of yoga grant souls both the four spiritual qualities and their diverse results.
items.plain_english: These givers of yoga, connected with the strands, bestow upon individual souls merit, knowledge, dispassion, lordship, and the various fruits that come from them.

rows.grounds: of the deity whose seat is the strands beginning with sattva
of the lord who is the consort of the one mother of the entire universe

items.question: Which world lies beyond the givers of yoga described earlier?
premises: There is a realm higher than those givers of yoga.
That realm belongs to the deity seated on the strands beginning with sattva.
That deity is Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, consort of the one mother of all worlds.
items.inference: Beyond the givers of yoga is the world of Lord Śrīkaṇṭha.
items.plain_english: Higher than them is the world of the god Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, who is seated on the strands beginning with sattva and is the lord of the one mother of the entire universe.

rows.grounds: by whom, in the worlds of Umā, Guha, Nīla, Brahmā, Ṛbhukṣa, Kṛta, Akṛta, and others
by the power taking the form of a seizing force
the beings presided over, beginning with Prabhu

items.question: How does Lord Śrīkaṇṭha act upon beings in the worlds below him?
premises: Lord Śrīkaṇṭha acts in the worlds of Umā, Guha, Nīla, Brahmā, Ṛbhukṣa, Kṛta, Akṛta, and others.
He acts through a power that takes the form of a seizing force.
Through that power he governs beings beginning with Prabhu.
items.inference: Śrīkaṇṭha presides over the beings of those worlds through his seizing power.
uncertainties: The exact nuance of graharūpiṇī is interpretive; it may suggest a controlling or possessing force.
items.plain_english: In the worlds of Umā, Guha, Nīla, Brahmā, Ṛbhukṣa, Kṛta, Akṛta, and others, he governs the beings beginning with Prabhu through his power in the form of a seizing force.

rows.grounds: desiring to withdraw the worlds here
who enters the lotus of the four-faced Brahmā
creates the worlds again up to the world of Jana

items.question: What cosmic act does Lord Śrīkaṇṭha perform through Brahmā?
premises: Desiring withdrawal, he enters the lotus of the four-faced Brahmā.
He burns the four worlds.
He creates the worlds again up to the world of Jana.
items.inference: Śrīkaṇṭha carries out cosmic dissolution and re-creation through Brahmā.
uncertainties: The identity of the four worlds burned is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: When he wishes to withdraw the worlds, he enters the lotus of the four-faced Brahmā, burns the four worlds, and then creates the worlds again up to the world of Jana.

rows.grounds: whose body consists of the strands beginning with sattva
there she is worshiped in every subsidiary cycle

items.question: How does Rudrāṇī participate in creation and worship according to Śrīkaṇṭha's will?
premises: By Śrīkaṇṭha's will, Rudrāṇī emits creation.
Rudrāṇī's body consists of the strands beginning with sattva.
In every subsidiary cycle, Rudrāṇī is worshiped on the altar.
items.inference: Rudrāṇī functions as both creative power and object of worship under Śrīkaṇṭha's will.
uncertainties: The ritual sense of vedī may be literal or symbolic.
items.plain_english: By his will, Rudrāṇī, whose body is made of the strands beginning with sattva, brings forth creation in each sub-cycle, and there Rudrāṇī is worshiped on the altar in every sub-cycle.

rows.grounds: then by Paśupati, Indra, Upendra, and Viriñci
and likewise made varied by gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, ancestors, and sages

items.question: Who performs the varied sacrifices connected with this worship?
premises: Paśupati, Indra, Upendra, and Viriñci perform sacrifices after receiving that worship.
The gods also perform sacrifices.
Gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, ancestors, and sages make the sacrifices varied.
items.inference: A wide range of divine and semi-divine beings participate in the sacrificial worship.
uncertainties: The exact object of tadupalambhataḥ is implied from the previous verse.
items.plain_english: Then Paśupati, Indra, Upendra, and Viriñci, having received that, perform sacrifices, and the gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, ancestors, and sages likewise perform varied forms of worship.

rows.grounds: above the level of the strands
the deities Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, and Saṃvarta
the deities Jyotiḥ, Piṅgala, and Sūraka

items.question: What is the unmanifest and which deities are located above the strands?
premises: The supreme equilibrium of the strands is the unmanifest.
Above the level of the strands there are specific deities.
Those deities include Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, Saṃvarta, Jyotiḥ, Piṅgala, and Sūraka.
items.inference: The unmanifest is defined as the balanced state of the strands, and above it dwell a group of Rudra deities.
items.plain_english: The supreme equilibrium of the strands is the unmanifest. Above the level of the strands are Krodheśa, Caṇḍa, Saṃvarta, Jyotiḥ, Piṅgala, and Sūraka.

rows.grounds: and Śikha and Uda, making eight

items.question: Which deities complete this group and what names describe the unmanifest there?
premises: Pañcāntaka and Ekavīra are in that realm.
Śikha and Uda complete a group of eight deities.
The unmanifest there is called dense, the resting place of the soul, primordial nature, root, and primary principle.
items.inference: The eight deities preside over the unmanifest, which is described by several synonymous names.
items.plain_english: There are also Pañcāntaka and Ekavīra, and with Śikha and Uda they make eight. In that realm the unmanifest is called the dense principle, the resting place of the soul, primordial nature, the root, and the primary principle.

rows.grounds: thus these are names for the cause of the strands
of that which originates from māyā
whose minds are tainted by both innate and adventitious impurity

items.question: What are these names synonyms for, and which souls are located there?
premises: The listed names are synonyms for the cause of the strands.
That principle belongs to the domain arising from māyā.
All souls whose minds are stained by innate and adventitious impurity are present there.
items.inference: The unmanifest, as the māyā-born cause of the strands, is the locus of impure individual souls.
items.plain_english: These are synonyms for the cause of the strands, which arises from māyā. All the individual souls whose minds are stained by both innate and adventitious impurity are located there.

rows.grounds: experiencing the enjoyments arising from that state
with instruments that are dull, manifest, or dissolved

items.question: How are the souls and Rudras situated in relation to their instruments in this realm?
premises: All those souls are placed there together with the Rudras.
They enjoy experiences arising from that state.
Some have dull, manifest, or dissolved instruments, while others are without instruments.
items.inference: Beings in this realm differ in whether and how they possess instruments of experience.
items.plain_english: All those souls are placed there, along with Rudras who enjoy the experiences arising from that state. Some have instruments that are dull, manifest, or dissolved, while others are without instruments.

rows.grounds: because they are not presided over or activated

items.question: How does the teaching define dull and manifest instruments?
premises: Instruments not governed are unable to act and are called dull.
Instruments that grasp fixed objects are clearly manifest.
The teaching calls these manifest instruments unfolded.
items.inference: The text distinguishes inactive dull instruments from active, object-specific manifest instruments.
items.plain_english: In the teaching, instruments that are not governed and cannot act are called dull. Those that grasp fixed objects and are clearly manifest are called unfolded.

rows.grounds: at the time of the great dissolution
and the effect is understood in the same way

items.question: What are dissolved and instrumentless states, and does the same apply to effects?
premises: Instruments broken in the great dissolution and not produced in creation are called dissolved.
Such states are dependent on will and are called instrumentless.
The same classification applies to effects.
items.inference: Dissolution, non-production, and will-dependence define instrumentless states for both instruments and effects.
items.plain_english: Instruments that are broken in the great dissolution and not produced at creation are called dissolved. Because they depend on will, they are also called instrumentless, and the same applies to effects.

rows.grounds: in the principle of the individual soul
prior to that or in front of that
indeed the eight worlds beginning with smallness

items.question: What groups are located in the principle of the individual soul?
premises: In the soul principle there is a ninefold group of satisfactions.
There are also eight accomplishments.
There are likewise eight worlds beginning with smallness.
items.inference: The soul principle contains parallel sets of satisfactions, accomplishments, and worlds.
uncertainties: The phrase tatpuraḥ is slightly ambiguous in spatial or sequential sense.
items.plain_english: In the principle of the individual soul there are nine satisfactions, eight accomplishments, and likewise the eight worlds beginning with smallness.

rows.grounds: in what is not truly the principle
through the idea that it is the principle
a sense of acceptability even in what should be rejected

items.question: How are satisfaction and accomplishment defined when based on a mistaken view of the principle?
premises: Contentment based on mistaking the non-principle for the principle is called satisfaction.
Such satisfaction takes what should be rejected as acceptable.
The followers of Kapila describe accomplishment in a corresponding way.
items.inference: Both satisfaction and accomplishment can arise from a mistaken identification of the true principle.
items.plain_english: When someone feels contentment by mistaking what is not the true principle for the principle, that is called satisfaction, and it treats what should be rejected as acceptable. The followers of Kapila describe accomplishment in the same way.

rows.grounds: named after nature, acquisition, time, and fortune
arising from withdrawal from objects due to earning, protecting, attachment, decay, and harm

items.question: What are the nine kinds of satisfaction mentioned in this classification?
premises: There are four internal satisfactions.
They are named after nature, acquisition, time, and fortune.
There are five more arising from withdrawal from objects because of earning, protecting, attachment, decay, and harm.
items.inference: The nine satisfactions consist of four internal types and five based on withdrawal from sense objects.
uncertainties: The compound in the fourth token is compressed and its exact parsing follows the traditional Sāṃkhya list.
items.plain_english: Four satisfactions are internal, named after nature, acquisition, time, and fortune. Five others arise from turning away from objects because of the troubles of earning, protecting, attachment, decay, and harm.

rows.grounds: obtaining a good friend or teacher

items.question: What are the eight accomplishments and what obstructs accomplishment?
premises: Reasoning, verbal testimony, and study are accomplishments.
The three removals of suffering, attainment of a friend, and giving complete the eight accomplishments.
The obstacle prior to accomplishment is threefold.
items.inference: Accomplishment has eight forms and is opposed by a threefold obstacle.
uncertainties: The exact nature of the threefold obstacle is not spelled out in this verse.
items.plain_english: The eight accomplishments are reasoning, verbal testimony, study, the three removals of suffering, gaining a good friend, and giving. The obstacle that comes before accomplishment is threefold.

rows.grounds: above the powers beginning with smallness there are three
because of association with the shadow of the three strands

items.question: What threefold rows exist above the powers beginning with smallness?
premises: Above the powers beginning with smallness there are three rows.
These rows pertain to teacher and student.
Their threefoldness is explained by association with the shadow of the three strands.
items.inference: The higher rows are triply divided in accordance with the influence of the three strands.
items.plain_english: Above the powers beginning with smallness there are three rows belonging to teacher and student. Even there, a threefold division is explained by their connection with the shadow of the three strands.

rows.grounds: beginning with iḍā and so on

items.question: What lies above the rows and what power is established in the soul there?
premises: Above the rows there is an eightfold group of channel-knowledges beginning with iḍā.
In the soul there is a power made of sound.
That power is called expansion.
items.inference: Beyond the rows, the soul is associated with an eightfold channel system and a sound-based expansive power.
uncertainties: The term nāḍīvidyāṣṭakaṃ may refer to channels, knowledges, or both.
items.plain_english: Above those rows is an eightfold group beginning with iḍā and the other channels. In the soul there is a sound-based power called expansion.

rows.grounds: for one who is not an agent
the soul cannot have the status of an agent
the state of being a cause
even if the soul is not an agent

items.question: Can the soul be a cause if it is not itself an agent?
premises: A non-agent soul cannot simply possess the causality of an agent.
Even if the soul is not an agent, it may be situated as a cooperating cause.
Causality must still be accounted for in relation to the soul.
items.inference: The soul's causality is explained not by direct agency but by its role as a cooperating cause.
items.plain_english: A soul that is not an agent cannot be established as the direct doer. Even if the soul is not an agent, it may still stand as a cooperating cause.

rows.grounds: otherwise one would have to accept that it becomes the rest of the effect
because the doctrine of the pre-existent effect would be undermined

items.question: Why must a special power of the soul be posited in relation to effects?
premises: If no such power is accepted, the soul would improperly become part of the effect.
That would undermine the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in its cause.
Therefore a specific power of the soul must be admitted in such effects.
items.inference: To preserve causal coherence, the soul must possess a distinct power operative in effects.
uncertainties: The compound śeṣakāryātmataiṣṭavyānyathā is dense and interpreted in line with the argument.
items.plain_english: Otherwise the soul would have to be taken as becoming part of the effect, which would damage the doctrine of the pre-existent effect. Therefore, in such a case, one must admit a specific power belonging to the soul.

rows.grounds: above the group of eight channels
the eightfold group of bodies is declared

items.question: How does the soul's power reach fullness and what is located above the eight channels?
premises: That power assumes as many forms as required.
By assuming those forms it attains fullness.
Above the eight channels an eightfold group of bodies is described.
items.inference: The soul's expansive power becomes complete through multiple forms, and above the channels lies an eightfold bodily grouping.
items.plain_english: Taking on that many forms, that power reaches fullness. Above the eight channels, an eightfold group of bodies is described.

rows.grounds: knowledge and the instruments that are to be accomplished
the eightfold set in the form of bodies
in the principle of the individual soul

items.question: What eight factors constitute the bodily grouping in the soul principle?
premises: The list includes effect, cause, suffering, and pleasure.
It also includes knowledge, what is to be accomplished, instruments, and means.
Together these form an eightfold bodily grouping in the soul principle.
items.inference: The eight bodies in the soul principle are defined by a set of experiential and causal factors.
uncertainties: The internal grouping implied by yuga in vigrahatāyugaṣṭakaṃ is not fully explicit.
items.plain_english: In the principle of the individual soul, the eightfold bodily grouping consists of effect, cause, suffering, pleasure, knowledge, what is to be accomplished, the instruments, and the means.

rows.grounds: continence, absence of deceit, and absence of anger

items.question: What world comes after the eight bodies and which bodily disciplines begin there?
premises: Beyond the eight bodies is the world of the ten bodily properties.
These properties include non-harm, truth, and non-stealing.
They also include continence, freedom from deceit, freedom from anger, and a discipline related to the teacher.
items.inference: After the eight bodies comes a realm defined by ten ethical and bodily disciplines.
uncertainties: The final element guroḥ is compressed; it likely refers to service or reverence to the teacher as part of the ten.
items.plain_english: Beyond the eight bodies is the world of the ten bodily disciplines: non-harm, truthfulness, non-stealing, continence, freedom from deceit, freedom from anger, and discipline in relation to the teacher.
